content: The following studies and their findings are summarized in a professional manner, focusing on their relevance to HIV prevention and infant feeding practices: 1. Crowley et al. (2015): This study evaluated the effectiveness of a national program in South Africa aimed at preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. However, it did not assess the specific outcomes of interest, such as HIV transmission rates. 2. Perez et al. (2004): The implementation of a rural PMTCT program in Zimbabwe was reviewed over an 18-month period. 3. Ciaranello et al.: This study did not address outcomes of interest related to exclusive breastfeeding or early breastfeeding initiation among HIV-positive mothers. 4. Freedberg (2013): The cost-effectiveness of the World Health Organization's 2010 PMTCT guidelines in Zimbabwe was analyzed. However, the study was not included in a systematic review due to its focus on cost rather than clinical outcomes. 5. Ladzani et al. (2011): This research provided data on the percentage of HIV-positive mothers who received infant feeding counseling in South Africa. However, it was unable to determine the proportion of mothers practicing exclusive breastfeeding. 6. Maman et al. (2012): The study explored infant feeding choices among HIV-positive women in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo. It provided limited information on breastfeeding promotion interventions. 7. Maru et al. (2009): This study examined the social determinants of mixed feeding behaviors among HIV-infected mothers in Nigeria. It did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 8. Muluye et al. (2012): The study investigated infant feeding practices among HIV-positive mothers in Ethiopia but did not evaluate interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 9. Zulliger et al. (2013): This mixed-methods study in Cape Town, South Africa, reported breastfeeding rates among HIV-positive women but did not specify whether breastfeeding was exclusive. 10. Petraro et al. (2011): Predictors of breastfeeding cessation among HIV-infected women in Tanzania were analyzed. The study did not address exclusive breastfeeding or early initiation outcomes. 11. Young et al. (2014): This study examined household food insecurity and maternal nutritional status among HIV-positive women in Uganda. It did not evaluate breastfeeding promotion interventions. 12. Onono et al. (2014): The study did not address exclusive breastfeeding promotion. 13. Kimunai et al. (2014): This research reviewed the relationship between maternal demographics and breastfeeding behavior among HIV-positive women in Kenya. It did not evaluate interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 14. Ssenyonga et al. (2004): The prevalence and factors associated with exclusive breastfeeding in Uganda were studied. However, the research did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 15. Lawani et al. (2014): Challenges in adherence to infant feeding choices in PMTCT programs in Nigeria were explored. The study did not evaluate exclusive breastfeeding promotion. 16. Berer (2003): This article discussed the limitations of traditional birth attendants in carrying out HIV prevention activities. It did not address breastfeeding promotion or outcomes of interest. 17. Andreson et al. (2013): A qualitative study on the infant feeding buddies strategy for HIV-positive mothers was conducted. While it addressed interventions, it did not provide outcomes of interest. 18. Buskens et al. (2007): This study explored infant feeding practices in Southern Africa but was not a clinical trial and did not address interventions or outcomes of interest. 19. Chisenga et al. (2011): Determinants of infant feeding choices among Zambian mothers were studied. The study could not determine the percentage of mothers practicing exclusive breastfeeding after receiving interventions. 20. Desclaux et al. (2009): This study examined counseling and decision-making regarding infant feeding options in resource-poor countries. It did not provide data on interventions or outcomes of interest. 21. Doherty et al. (2006): A longitudinal study in South Africa explored infant feeding decision-making among HIV-positive women. It did not provide information on interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 22. Madiba et al. (2013): Barriers to PMTCT in South Africa were assessed, with implications for infant feeding practices. The study did not address exclusive breastfeeding promotion. 23. Mahaka et al. (2008): Knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding infant feeding among HIV-positive mothers were reviewed. The study did not provide data on outcomes of interest. 24. Nor et al. (2012): This study assessed mothers' perceptions of peer counseling interventions in South Africa. It did not address outcomes of interest. 25. Petrovic et al. (2009): Knowledge about PMTCT among first-time mothers in Zambia was studied. The research did not address outcomes of interest. 26. Seidel et al. (2000): Experiences of breastfeeding among HIV-positive women in Durban were explored. The study did not address outcomes of interest. 27. Sibeko et al. (2009): Constraints and supports for optimal infant feeding in an HIV-impacted urban community in South Africa were assessed. The study did not address outcomes of interest. 28. Bezner Kerr et al. (2008): The role of grandmothers in infant feeding practices in Malawi was explored. The study did not address outcomes of interest. 29. Buskens et al. (2008): The study evaluated infant feeding counseling encounters in Southern Africa. It did not address outcomes of interest. 30. Nor et al. (2009): Peer counseling in high HIV prevalence areas was studied. The research did not address outcomes of interest. 31. Sripipatana et al. (2007): Site-specific interventions to improve PMTCT programs in less developed settings were reviewed. The study highlighted qualitative program aspects but did not address outcomes of interest. 32. Våga et al. (2014): This study reflected on informed choice in infant feeding counseling in Tanzania. It compared interventions but did not focus on outcomes of interest. 33. Østergaard et al. (2010): Exclusive breastfeeding among HIV-positive mothers in Malawi was studied. The research did not provide information on interventions of interest. 34. Thairu et al.: Sociocultural influences on infant feeding decisions among HIV-infected women in South Africa were explored. The study provided limited information on interventions and outcomes of interest. 35. Sellen et al. (2007): Client experiences with safe infant feeding counseling in Kenya were reviewed. The study did not provide information on interventions or outcomes of interest. 36. Saloojee et al. (2010): A review article on infant feeding among HIV-positive mothers was conducted. It did not provide specific outcomes of interest. 37. Bhandari et al. (2008): This review article focused on scaling up exclusive breastfeeding in maternal and child health programs. It did not provide specific outcomes of interest. 38. Rollins et al. (2013): A review article on breastfeeding and HIV transmission in the developing world was conducted. It did not provide specific outcomes of interest. 39. Tomlinson et al. (2014): This randomized controlled trial (RCT) demonstrated low risk of bias and adequate follow-up, with prespecified outcomes reported. 40. Bland et al. (2008): This cohort study assessed infant feeding practices but did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 41. Iliff et al. (2005): This cohort study evaluated infant feeding practices but did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 42. Mazia et al. (2009): This cohort study assessed infant feeding practices but did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 43. Piwowz et al. (2005, 2007): These studies reviewed infant feeding practices but did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 44. Suryavanshi et al. (2003): This cohort study assessed infant feeding practices but did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 45. Thakwalakwa et al. (2014): This cohort study assessed infant feeding practices but did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding. 46. Bii et al. (2008): This cross-sectional study assessed infant feeding practices but did not address interventions promoting exclusive breastfeeding.
